The research tool hit its usage limit after that page. I found the Pulpit Commentary, the Bible Hub verse pages and StudyLight in search results, but couldn't open them. So these notes don't cover Gill, Ellicott, Precept Austin, NET Bible, the Catholic and Orthodox sites, or any comparison between traditions. Guzik does quote many other writers (Maclaren, Feinberg, Trapp, Harrison, Thompson, Kidner, Morgan, Clarke, Cundall, Schaeffer). Those quotes are given below as he presents them. I didn't check them against the original works.

All points come from https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-37/

**Part 1: The traditional reading**

**vv. 1–2**
- Coniah is another name for Jehoiachin. He reigned only a few months in 598 BC, because Nebuchadnezzar came against Jerusalem a second time.
- After removing Coniah, Nebuchadnezzar made Coniah's uncle, Zedekiah, king. Zedekiah still didn't use his position to listen to God or to Jeremiah.
- Maclaren calls Zedekiah a weak man put in charge at a moment that would have tested the strongest ruler.
- Feinberg notes that Zedekiah had promised loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar. Pressure from a pro-Egypt party at court made him break that promise, and this led directly to the final siege.
- Jeremiah's message being ignored was this: Babylon would conquer Judah, resisting was useless, and the people should surrender and accept God's correction.

**v. 3**
- The siege was so bad that a king who wouldn't listen to God asked for prayer and even called the LORD "our God." Desperation drove the request.
- Trapp says Zedekiah seems somewhat better than his brother Jehoiakim. But he was a hypocrite: he wanted the prophet's prayers while refusing to obey his preaching.

**v. 4**
- Guzik points to Jeremiah 32:1 and following for the imprisonment that came later.

**v. 5**
- When the Babylonians left to face Egypt, it looked to Zedekiah like a miracle and an answer to prayer.
- Harrison identifies this Pharaoh as Hophra (see Jer. 44:30), who reigned 589–570 BC. He marched rashly to support Zedekiah's revolt (Ezek. 17:11–21) but pulled back before fighting. Jerusalem then fell in 587 BC.

**vv. 6–8**
- God's answer was that Egypt would go home without standing against Babylon, so hoping for Egyptian help was pointless. The Babylonians would come back, take the city and burn it.

**vv. 9–10**
- The picture of wounded men getting up from their tents shows there was no way Babylon could fail. Even an army of nothing but wounded soldiers would still take and burn the city.

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik links this trip to the land Jeremiah bought in Jer. 32:6–12, a sign of God's promise to restore Judah. With the siege lifted, Jeremiah could go and see it.
- Thompson says the Hebrew phrase translated "claim his portion" is unclear. He suggests the family inheritance was being discussed because of the invasion, and Jeremiah was on his way to a family meeting about dividing it.

**v. 13**
- Jeremiah had said resisting Babylon was useless, so people suspected he sided with Babylon, perhaps even as a spy.
- Thompson notes that Jeremiah had urged people to desert (Jer. 21:9; 38:2), and some Judeans really did go over to the enemy (38:19; 52:15). So Irijah's charge was understandable, though wrong.

**vv. 14–15**
- Jeremiah was beaten and jailed. Clarke stresses there was no proof and no fair process.
- These officials came about fifteen years after the friendly officials of Jer. 36:11–19. A new generation had no sympathy for Jeremiah.
- Harrison says the scribe's house was a makeshift prison, and cisterns were sometimes used to hold prisoners (compare 38:6, 13).
- Feinberg suggests Jonathan's house was used because Jeremiah was one of many deserters and political prisoners being held.

**v. 16**
- Trapp explains the Hebrew as a pit or hole where the prisoner could neither walk nor lie down properly.
- Kidner asks whether the king hoped the "many days" would break Jeremiah's spirit.
- Guzik observes that no false prophets were in that prison, because their message pleased the rulers.

**v. 17**
- Zedekiah asked in secret because he didn't want it known that he doubted the prophets who promised good news.
- Morgan sees the secrecy as a sign of fear: for all his weakness, the king knew God's power.
- Duhm, quoted by Thompson, describes Zedekiah as more bound than the prisoner standing in front of him.
- Guzik's application: God's message was the same in private as in public. Zedekiah wrongly hoped for a secret word that differed from what God had already said. Guzik allows that God may give an individual a personal word, but says believers should not seek a secret word and should look to Scripture instead.
- Cundall says a prophet who had stood firm for forty years was not going to give way now.

**vv. 18–19**
- The false prophets' prediction had plainly failed. That showed Jeremiah's only "crime" was telling the truth.
- Schaeffer, quoted via Ryken, warns that faithful preachers in a post-Christian world may end up like Jeremiah.

**v. 20**
- This was an earnest plea to be spared the terrible conditions in Jonathan's house. Guzik notes that conditions in the courtyard of the guard (32:1–2) were much better.

**v. 21**
- Zedekiah respected Jeremiah's honesty, so he moved him somewhere more humane and gave him daily bread.
- Guzik's application: people being persecuted may rightly try to improve their conditions. Nothing commands them to accept the worst without appeal.
- Maclaren says Zedekiah knew Jeremiah was innocent and should have obeyed God, but was too much of a coward to stand up to his officials.
- Kidner thinks the king's motives were mixed, and he didn't want this man of God's death on his hands.
- Trapp holds that God rewarded this kindness by giving Zedekiah a natural death and an honourable burial in Babylon.
